Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-17 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Martin (CTO - Crestline Health), Priya Rao (Lead Engineer), Marcus Lee (Platform Eng)
Recording ID: fireflies-20260517-8732

Summary: quick hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation basics. Emphasis on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), backpressure and retry strategies, and a short console/Optimize tour. Customer is health-tech so security/VPC questions surfaced.

Topics: [1] Streaming semantics and reconnects [2] Retry/backoff + idempotency tokens [3] Console quick tour + Optimize recommendations [4] Cost/latency tradeoffs and dedicated vs hosted scenario (brief)

Action items mentioned in call (quick): send sandbox, run benchmark, share security pack, follow-up infra call.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery (AE): Hey everybody, thanks for joining. I think we have about 45 minutes, we'll run through a short hosted API demo, show streaming, then Samir will jump into retries and a quick console tour.
[00:18] Jules (CTO): Great, appreciate it. We're primarily curious about latency and how graceful failures are, since we have PHI-ish traffic, so VPC and audit logs matter.
[00:28] Avery: Yes, totally. We'll call out the VPC options and SOC2 artifacts at the end. Quick intro—Samir, want to kick off streaming demo?
[00:32] Samir (SE): Sure. I'll share my screen, starting with the basic chat call to /v1/generate (note: we used a dev token). You'll see streaming chunks via SSE here—it's chunked tokens as they arrive.
[00:48] Samir: (typing) sample request: model: redwood-2-chat, messages: [system, user], temperature .2, top_p .9, max_tokens 256, stream true; we'll also pass client_id and idempotency_token for the example.
[01:12] Priya: Can you explain idempotency_token again? We have some frontend retries and need to avoid duplicate charges or duplicate user messages.
[01:19] Samir: Yep—idempotency_token ties a client request to a server-side attempt, so if the client retries we detect duplicates. In streaming, you get partial chunks but the server asserts dedup at completion. Also we show how to resume a stream using last_event_id in some cases. Note: resume is not perfect for context > 8k, so we recommend small session-level checkpoints.
[01:44] Marcus: When you say resume not perfect, is it KV cache related? We have a lot of long conversation state.
[01:50] Samir: Good question—two things: KV cache (we sometimes see it transcribed as K-V cash in older notes) is kept in-memory on the runner; resumes require supplying a consistent convo context or using prefix-KV snapshots. For long histories we recommend doing prefix caching on the client side and only streaming recent deltas.
[02:12] [00:02:12] Avery: Quick demo break — I'm going to intentionally simulate a mid-stream disconnect to show retry behavior.
[02:22] Samir: (runs a small script) triggering a simulated network drop; notice the client reconnect logic has exponential backoff + jitter. If the reconnect uses same idempotency token it will either resume or start a safe fallback path.
[02:40] Priya: If the stream reconnects and sends overlapping tokens, do we get dedup automatically or do we need to implement client-side de-dupe?
[02:47] Samir: Server-side dedup handles full-request duplicates. For partial overlaps we recommend making the client do a simple last-n-token check—practical approach is to include sequence offsets in the streaming chunks.
[03:05] Jules: Are there SDK helpers for that? We have a react native app and it's messy to manage reconnects.
[03:12] Samir: Yes — our JS SDK wraps stream reconnection and exposes a small onDelta hook with delta.sequence and delta.partialText so you can stitch safely. The SDK also provides an idempotency helper and a persistence example in the quickstart.
[03:30] Avery: Moving on to parameters—temperature, top_p, max_tokens. Quick cheat: temperature controls randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling and can give different failure modes. For deterministic results we recommend temp 0.0 and top_p 0.0 for exactness (but you lose creativity).
[03:52] Priya: We're mostly doing summarization & Triage classification so low temp makes sense. Are there any batching tricks we should consider?
[04:00] Samir: Yes—if you have many small requests, batching at the runtime reduces per-token cost dramatically. We have continuous batching where the runtime groups similar sequence-length requests and schedules them on the same GPU batch. In Console -> Optimize we can show batching recommendations per workload.
[04:22] Marcus: Relatedly, how does backpressure work—if our client sends bursts during a shift change?
[04:29] Samir: The runtime enforces per-route rate limits and latency SLOs. For sudden bursts, the system may queue or redirect to burst capacity. On client-side we recommend implementing an adaptive window: look at token-per-second feedback and back off, or implement a token-leaky bucket. The console has a traffic view so you can tune thresholds.
[04:52] [00:04:52] Avery: Ok console tour now—Samir, can you pull up the Optimize recommendations?
[05:00] Samir: (shares console) Here's a sample Optimize page: suggestions show model quantization, recommended batch_size, prefix-cache hit rate and cost savings estimates. For this demo I'm toggling a suggestion to try int8 quantized runner which drops cost ~30% in the example.
[05:22] Jules: Any tradeoffs with quantization on hallucinations/quality? We can't degrade diagnoses.
[05:28] Samir: Yes—quant can affect output distribution slightly. Optimize includes a quality regression alert tied to your eval prompts; if the metric drops we suggest rolling back or using a higher precision runner for critical routes. For regulated workflows we recommend a quality gate before applying quantization automatically.
[05:50] Priya: Do you store prompts or user PII in logs? We need to avoid PHI leaking to logs.
[05:56] Avery: By default hosted logs are redacted at token-level per your retention policy; for PHI we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with a VPC and customer-managed KMS. We'll share SOC2 artifacts and log-retention configs.
[06:14] Marcus: Good. Can you run a quick failure-mode demo—what happens when model endpoint OOMs or runner is saturated?
[06:20] Samir: Sure—simulating runner OOM. See here: the API returns a 503 with a structured error and an optional fallback model id. We showed earlier how routing policies can fallback to a smaller model (e.g., redwood-lite) automatically. Also the runtime can return partial output plus an error flag so client can decide to use partial result or queue for re-request.
[06:46] Priya: If we fall back to smaller model, will semantics change and break downstream parsers?
[06:52] Samir: Potentially yes—that's why we support pinned model versions and a canary rollout. In Console you can define a schema/regression test; if fallback model fails the check the system can route to another pool or raise an alert.
[07:12] [00:07:12] Avery: Quick interjection—competitors question, Jules?
[07:15] Jules: I did have a note—how is this materially different vs OpenAI managed endpoints or Anthropic?
[07:22] Avery: Main difference is we design for predictable inference economics and deployment options: hosted for speed, dedicated for throughput, private for compliance. Plus the Optimize layer gives actionable batching and quantization suggestions tied to cost/quality.
[07:36] Samir: Also our streaming semantics and reconnect helpers are more prescriptive—we publish a reconnection playbook with sample code and idempotency patterns.
[07:48] Marcus: Back to retries—what pattern do you recommend? Exponential backoff + jitter and how many retries?
[07:55] Samir: Standard: try 3 attempts with exponential backoff (100ms, 300ms, 900ms) with jitter. For idempotent requests you can be more aggressive; for non-idempotent you need server-side dedup or client confirmation. For streaming we prefer to fail-fast and let client re-request with same idempotency token rather than blind retries mid-stream.
[08:18] Priya: Are there server-side metrics for duplicate detection? We need to prove no double-billing.
[08:22] Avery: Yes—billing events are deduped server-side and included in audit logs; we can provide export examples.
[08:30] [00:08:30] Samir: Ok I'm going to show a simulated reconnect flow. Notice the client picks up last_event_id:42 and asks for resume; the server replies with missing token 43-50 and continues. If resume isn't possible we fall back to full re-request using idempotency token to avoid double-processing.
[08:55] Jules: Does that require sticky routing to the same runner?
[08:58] Samir: For resume yes, sticky session makes it simpler but it's not required; we persist prefix snapshots to enable resume across runners within the same deployment group.
[09:12] Marcus: Nice. Any observability hooks for latency per-token?
[09:16] Samir: Console exposes per-route p50/p95/p99 token latency, and you can instrument traces with our SDK to see token-level timings. There's also a trace-id header you can pass to correlate with your logs.
[09:30] Priya: For our compliance team, can we get a sample audit log format?
[09:34] Avery: We'll attach the SOC2 + sample audit log export as part of the next steps.
[09:40] [00:09:40] Samir: Switching to the Optimize suggestions: here's a real example where we detected low prefix-cache hit rate; Optimize suggested increasing the prefix-cache window from 128 tokens to 512 which reduced per-request tokens by ~12%.
[09:58] Priya: Is prefix-cache client-side or server-side?
[10:01] Samir: It's server-side with optional client hints. The runtime stores hot KV cache; client can hint which parts are stable and we maintain a fingerprint to validate.
[10:14] Jules: You mentioned dedicated vs hosted earlier—when should we think about Dedicated given our throughput?
[10:19] Avery: If you need SLAs and predictable throughput with private networking, Dedicated is the next step. For many teams, start hosted, then when you hit consistent >X qps or strict data residency needs, we propose a Dedicated commit. We'll work with finance for commit sizing.
[10:35] Marcus: Do you offer prewarmed pools for peak times?
[10:38] Samir: Yes—prewarmed runner pools and burst capacity options. Console lets you schedule prewarm windows to avoid cold-starts during known peaks.
[10:48] [00:10:48] Avery: Alright, small interactive part—Samir will trigger a controlled failure and show how client should surface a graceful message to users.
[10:55] Samir: (runs script) failure turned on. Client receives 5xx with error_code:runner_unavailable; we annotate the UI suggestion: "Temporary service interruption — we are retrying" and show a progress spinner. In our sample SDK we provide an onError hook to map error_codes to UX flows.
[11:18] Priya: What about partial responses—should we cache them and show to user? We have triage flows where partial is acceptable.
[11:24] Samir: If partial is acceptable you can surface it; we return partial + error flag. If downstream parsers expect strict schema, don't accept partial unless you validate. Console-based schema checks can be used as gate.
[11:40] Jules: Can we run a short spike to measure median token latency under our expected payload?
[11:45] Avery: Yes — that's one of the next steps. Samir will provision a sandbox and run a 2-hour spike with their sample prompts.
[11:55] [00:11:55] Samir: Quick note on rate-limiting headers—X-RateLimit-Remaining per-route and Retry-After are provided. If you see Retry-After, best to back off and respect the header.
[12:08] Marcus: For the sandbox, will it have data egress restrictions? We need no PHI leaving our VPC.
[12:14] Avery: Hosted sandbox won't be appropriate for PHI. For a PHI-safe test, we can provision a Dedicated trial or Private with network controls; we'll discuss offline with legal.
[12:28] Priya: Understood.
[12:30] [00:12:30] Samir: A couple more tips: 1) For structured outputs use function/tool calling or structured output mode to reduce parsing errors. 2) Use evals tied to console alerts so you detect drift post-quantization.
[12:50] Priya: Do you support tool-calling style JSON responses? We rely on JSON schema.
[12:55] Samir: Yes, the chat endpoint supports structured output enforcement and a schema mode—if the model violates schema the call returns a validation error and the output is flagged.
[13:08] Jules: Any example of costs savings with batching and quantization combined?
[13:12] Samir: In one example we reduced per-token cost by ~45% by combining 2x batching and int8 runners; but again, monitor quality via evals.
[13:28] [00:13:28] Avery: Ok last ~30 minutes we'll open for Q&A and then recap next steps.
[13:34] Priya: A question about idempotency across multiple frontends — is the idempotency token global across customers?
[13:40] Samir: It's scoped to the API key + token combo. If you have multiple frontends behind a single API key we recommend generating per-client idempotency tokens that include a client prefix.
[13:56] Marcus: If we do private deployment, do we still get Optimize recommendations?
[14:00] Avery: Yes — Private deployments can opt-in to the Optimize control plane or run a local agent that computes suggestions. For sensitive customers we offer the latter.
[14:14] [00:14:14] Jules: Ok I have a last compliance question — do you integrate with our KMS (Azure Key Vault)?
[14:18] Avery: Yes we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for Private and Dedicated; for hosted we support envelope encryption with customer-managed keys via partner integrations. We'll include a KMS integration note in the security pack.
[14:36] Priya: Great.
[14:38] Samir: Final quick note on retries and idempotency: if you implement retry-after with exponential backoff and always send idempotency tokens, you'll be covered for billing and dedupe. Also include a short server-side reconciliation job once a day to confirm no duplicates.
[14:58] Jules: Makes sense.
[15:00] [00:15:00] Avery: Ok recap and next steps: 1) We will send sandbox creds and quickstart; 2) Send SOC2 + VPC/KMS whitepaper; 3) Samir runs a benchmark with their sample prompts; 4) schedule infra deep-dive (May 25 proposed). Anything else?
[15:18] Priya: Please include the SDK reconnection example in the quickstart.
[15:22] Avery: Will do.
[15:24] Marcus: Can you also send a short spreadsheet template for traffic profile?
[15:28] Avery: Yes.
[15:30] Jules: Thanks, this was helpful.
[15:32] Avery: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
